headline: Patrick William flags systemic risk in property development-focused private credit funds following the Bethel Group case, warning of significant redemption pressure and reputational damage.
reasoning: William highlights the Bethel Group (also referred to as Ben Butler) case in New South Wales as a cautionary example of herding behaviour in property development lending, where funds abandoned pre-sales requirements because peers were doing so — substituting 'market practice' for independent credit judgment. He expects a wave of redemptions to hit the sector, with good and bad funds punished alike, leading to a broader industry shakeup. The root cause, in his view, is programmatic or templated underwriting that removes individual investment judgment and causes managers to replicate each other's mistakes rather than applying rigorous analysis.
quote: It's still under investigation. So I think the fallout for those funds, unfortunately, is a slew of redemptions. So people are very, very concerned. So there'll be a shakeup of the industry. And I suspect some of those funds, you know, the good funds will be punished, maybe unfairly. The not so good funds will be punished fairly, but you'll see a lot of pain in that sector... a lot of those sales to Bethel had zero pre-sales, and I suspect it's because everyone else is doing it, so we should do it as well. If anyone asked we'll say well that's market, but that's not good enough if you're managing someone else's capital.

headline: Rixon Capital's Patrick William warns that loan count alone does not equal genuine diversification in private credit portfolios.
reasoning: Patrick William argues that apparent diversification in private credit is illusory if underlying loans share correlated exposures — for example, 200 loans to property developers in New South Wales effectively constitute a single large exposure. He draws an analogy to private equity, where even large funds hold only 10–40 positions because deep due diligence takes time and requires judgment. He stresses that investors should scrutinise whether the underwriting team is large enough relative to the fund size to conduct genuine, judgment-based analysis rather than templated, tick-box processes. If a small team is deploying a large pool of capital quickly, the quality of underwriting is likely to be degraded.
quote: So you got 200 loans to property developers in New South Wales. It's actually one big exposure. And the implicit assumption is you've actually underwritten those positions very well, as opposed to using a template and machine gunning money out of the market... So the question that investors should ask is if you've got $1 billion portfolio with 400 loans, how many people have you actually got underwriting it? Because if it's a big team, fair enough. Odds are you're running the full gamut of judgment and detailed due diligence. But if it's a small team, odds are that due diligence is templated. You tick five boxes, the borrower is going to get themselves a check.

headline: Corporate private credit requires team size commensurate with fund size and genuine investment judgment, not AI-driven templating
reasoning: William distinguishes corporate private credit as a segment where the complexity of borrowers — ranging from HVAC businesses to marine construction companies — demands experienced human judgment that AI cannot replicate. He acknowledges AI has a useful role in processing and compiling information but insists final credit decisions must rely on 10–20 years of sector experience and direct management engagement. The key investor due-diligence question is whether the investment team's headcount is sufficient relative to the fund's portfolio size to allow individual, thoughtful underwriting of each loan.
quote: So with corporate private credit, what you want to see is a team that matches the size of the fund. So not a five man team running $1 billion fund. You want to know there's enough manpower that the underwriting is detailed and, you know, there's actual judgment... if you're lending to a HVAC business, you're lending to a marine construction business. AI can only do so much. At the end of the day, you are hinging on, or investors are actually hinging on the investment team's judgment. Ten, 15, 20 years of experience. I've seen this before. I've seen the risks. So AI will compile the information for you, but it is on you to do that research, analyze it and make that final decision.

headline: Bathla Group fallout will expose poor underwriting practices and fee-driven lending decisions across private credit funds over next 6–12 months
reasoning: Patrick William believes the Bathla Group situation will act as a sorting mechanism for the private credit industry, revealing which funds underwrote loans on sound credit versus those motivated by attractive upfront fees to the fund manager. He highlights the importance of the basis on which loans were made — as-if-complete valuations versus other bases — as a key differentiator. He expects the full picture to emerge over the next 6 to 12 months, effectively stress-testing fund manager quality across the sector.
quote: I think this will sort the wheat from the chaff, because the whole range of funds and some of them are good funds with great reputations. So what will come on the wash is what levers each of those funds lent out. Was it on an as if complete basis or as if basis? The big difference there? Um, and more controversially, you might see some funds caught up where the loan wasn't made because the credit was good, but it was because the upfront fees to the fund manager were attractive. And I think all that'll come out in the wash the next 6 to 12 months.
episode_title: The $3.2B warning sign for private credit

headline: Bathla Group's $3.2B debt load signals systemic stress in Australian private credit property development sector
reasoning: Patrick William flags Bathla Group, a NSW property developer carrying $3.2B in debt against just $33M in cash, as a significant warning sign for the Australian private credit market. He describes the sheer scale as likely to spook the market, with 18 lenders averaging $150M exposure each. He expects more distressed developers to emerge given rising costs, weak demand for new builds in aspirational suburbs, and affordability constraints on the target buyer demographic. He believes the episode will sort the wheat from the chaff across private credit funds, exposing those who lent on poor credit quality in pursuit of upfront fees.
quote: I'd like to think it's one big cockroach rather than a box full of cockroaches. But I think the concern with this one is just the sheer scale. You know, you'll always have a developer or business here or there struggle. It's part of doing business. And you know, it comes with all business. Lending comes with the risk. But I think the sheer scale of this one is going to spook the market.
episode_title: The $3.2B warning sign for private credit

headline: Australian property development private credit faces further defaults as costs rise and buyer demand weakens
reasoning: Patrick William expects more property developers to come under stress, citing budget blowouts, increased construction costs, and insufficient demand for new builds in western suburban and aspirational locations. He notes the target market — young buyers in aspirational suburbs — is being squeezed by wage stagnation and rising rates, reducing their ability to qualify for mortgages. He believes most developer loan-to-value ratios are likely higher than funds would want them to be.
quote: I suspect so. Um, you know, the way the budgets come out, the way the economy is performed, the way the costs have increased. I suspect most of these are higher than what the funds want them to be. Number one and number two, um, you know, the demand for those investment properties aren't there because a lot of people want to buy properties that are existing because, you know, the quality is good. So the target market for all these western suburb developments in more aspirational suburbs are young people. But if your salary has an increase in rates are on track to go up. Odds are you may not qualify for that long.
episode_title: The $3.2B warning sign for private credit

headline: High-quality Australian corporate private credit remains sound and is likely where AustralianSuper is increasing exposure
reasoning: Patrick William draws a sharp distinction between property development lending and corporate private credit, noting that cash-flow lenders to high-quality profitable Australian corporates are performing well. He interprets AustralianSuper's reported move to increase private credit exposure as targeting the corporate and high-quality lending segment, and potentially opportunistic lending in other geographies, rather than domestic property development. He emphasises the nuance within the private credit label that can be lost in headline coverage.
quote: Well, there's a lot of nuance to that. So that's a good. So the headline can be misleading. So it is private credit. But there's a lot of subsegments within that private credit sector. So we're an asset backed corporate lender. We're not exposed to things like that. You've got cash flow lenders that lend to high quality, profitable Australian corporates. Those businesses are doing perfectly fine. So I suspect Aussie Super is looking to increase exposure to the corporate, the high quality corporate lending side of the market and perhaps opportunistic lens in other geographies, but probably not property development in this country.
episode_title: The $3.2B warning sign for private credit
